source.title: DualEdit: Mitigating Safety Fallback in LLM Backdoor Editing via Affirmation-Refusal Regulation
source.authors: Hou-Cheng Jiang; Zetong Zhao; Jun-Feng Fang; Hao-Kai Ma; Rui-Peng Wang; Xiang Wang; Xiang-Nan He; Yang Deng

record.tranche_reason: The study builds a backdoor-editing method around the safety-fallback phenomenon and reports attack and fallback outcomes under that deliberate edit. It does not test the claim’s fine-tuning, aligned-versus-base KL, compliant-prefill, or safety-training interventions.
record.gate_note: The reported attack success and safety-fallback results are for harmful prompts with an intentionally injected backdoor; they do not establish that these behaviors arise without that inducement. The paper also discusses mid-generation refusal probabilities, but gives no extractable numerical values for the figure.
record.test_reason: This is a backdoor-injection method paper. It deliberately edits weights so a trigger maps to compliance, and its headline results compare DualEdit's attack success and safety-fallback rates with other editing baselines. It does not fine-tune on harmful or benign data (V1/V2), measure aligned-vs-base per-token KL (V3), or test prefilling, suffix or decoding attacks (V4). It does not localize where safety lives (V5), examine causes of shallowness (V6), or train deeper alignment (V7). Its one relevant observation is that baseline edits often start with 'Sure' and then revert to refusal. That bears on the related idea of how far a compliant opening carries, but under trigger-based weight editing rather than prefilling, so it is recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors argue that affirmation-only editing attacks suffer 'safety fallback' (mid-generation refusal). They report that DualEdit, which combines affirmative promotion and refusal suppression with dynamic loss weighting and value anchoring, raises triggered ASR by about 10% and lowers SFR by about 11% over baselines. They also report that general capability drops by under 1.48% on average.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses localized trigger-based parameter editing with affirmative-token promotion and refusal-token suppression, rather than fine-tuning or measuring aligned-versus-base per-token KL.
record.method_sensitivity: Attack outcomes vary with trigger position and choice, the number of target nodes, and the penalty coefficient λ; the paper also discusses editing-layer choices.

fits_no_version.finding: Affirmation-only backdoor edits (BadEdit, ROME, MEMIT, JailbreakEdit) often make models open with 'Sure' and then refuse mid-generation. The paper calls this 'safety fallback'. Refusal-token probability rises around positions 10–27 (Fig. 3; Obs 4), and case studies show 'Sure, I cannot provide...' outputs. Suppressing refusal tokens as well as promoting affirmation reduces this fallback.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: When a compliant opening is induced by weight editing rather than prefilling, safety-aligned models frequently recover and refuse later in generation. An affirmative first token alone does not reliably bypass safety under this kind of intervention.

record.problems: The headline attack and fallback outcomes are measured under an intentionally injected backdoor, so they do not establish spontaneous compliance or test the claim’s fine-tuning and prefill mechanisms. The aggregate statements provide no uncertainty estimates. The paper describes refusal-token probability plots, but the figure values are not numerically extractable from the text.
record.rows_left_out: Per-model and per-dataset table entries and ablation values are not separately cataloged here; the extracted rows are the explicit aggregate outcomes in Section 4.2. The qualitative Figure 3 descriptions are noted in gate_note but have no extractable numerical values.

untested.parts: Fine-tuning on harmful examples; the study uses rank-one trigger edits, not fine-tuning.
Per-token KL between aligned and base models.
Prefilling a compliant start, adversarial suffixes, decoding changes. Only weight-edit-induced affirmative openings are studied.
Whether safety itself is carried by few weights. The single-layer edit injects a trigger mapping and does not localize safety.
Data or objective causes of shallowness.
Training that deepens safety beyond the first tokens.

record.verdict_notes: Mid-generation refusal after an affirmative opening is loosely related to V4. However, the opening is induced by a backdoor weight edit, not prefilling, and the study's goal is attack performance. The rules exclude both deliberate inducement and method-vs-baseline comparisons from verdicts. Table 1 gives per-model SFR for the baseline editors; e.g. LLaMA-2-7B DAN: 37.7–43.6% vs DualEdit 18.2%. The anomalously high pre-edited SFRs (e.g. 84.62%, 95.63%) suggest SFR is not cleanly conditional on an affirmative start, which limits its use for any version. The paper cites Qi et al. 2024 (arXiv:2406.05946) as background only.

versions.untested_parts: Fine-tuning on harmful examples and its effect on refusal.
Fine-tuning on ordinary or carefully chosen benign data.
Per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models on harmful prompts.
Prefilling a compliant opening, suffix attacks, and decoding changes; the paper instead studies trigger-based parameter editing.
Whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behavior.
Whether the safety-training data or objective causes shallow safety behavior.
Training that spreads safety beyond the first tokens and its robustness.

rows.check: Own-method-vs-baseline SFR reduction (10.88%). 'Partial' has no version to refer to. The SFR definition is also ambiguous: pre-edited models score SFR of 75–98% (Table 1) even though unedited models rarely open affirmatively, so SFR values cannot be read as fallback-after-affirmation rates.
